target.task: Our private university in Dhaka has one 400-space car park for staff and students. Most cars arrive between 8:00 and 10:00, the car park is about half empty after 14:00, and it is almost empty after 19:00. Design the weekday parking fee schedule for 7:00 to 22:00.

rules.text: Use 3 or 4 time periods that together cover 7 to 22 without gaps, with whole-hour start and end times.
Each period has one fee per entry in whole BDT, from 0 to 100.
Include a monthly staff pass priced at no more than 1500 BDT.

target.format: Reply with JSON only, in this shape: {"periods": [{"label": "...", "start_hour": 7, "end_hour": 10, "fee_bdt": 0}], "staff_monthly_pass_bdt": 0}

source_example.text: Stockholm ran congestion charges as a full-scale trial from 3 January to 31 July 2006. After a referendum in September 2006, in which a majority of city voters said yes, the charges became permanent on 1 August 2007. The charge was collected at 18 control points on the roads into and out of the inner city. Cameras read each car's number plate, so drivers did not have to stop. The price depended on the time of day. A passage in the busiest half hours cost 20 Swedish kronor (SEK), the shoulder periods around them cost 15 SEK, and the remaining daytime periods cost 10 SEK. No charge applied in the evening, at night, at weekends or on public holidays. A driver paid at most 60 SEK in one day, however often they crossed the cordon. Traffic across the cordon fell by about 20 percent compared with the year before, and queues on the main approach roads became much shorter. Planners explained the result simply: drivers who could move their trip to a cheaper half hour, or to public transport, did so. The through route Essingeleden was exempt at first, because it was the main bypass around the centre. Residents of the island of Lidingö also had an exemption at the start, since their only road link to the mainland ran through the charged zone. Public support was low before the trial and rose after people saw the shorter queues. The revenue was earmarked for transport investment in the Stockholm region. Later evaluations found that the traffic reduction lasted for years after the charges became permanent. The charges were raised in 2016, and Essingeleden began to be charged at the same time. Researchers have used the case to argue that a price which follows the daily peak can manage scarce road space better than a flat price. Critics pointed to the cost of running the camera system and asked whether a simpler flat fee would have worked. The Stockholm design is a three-step price ladder in which the top price is double the bottom one. It also shows that a daily cap protects people who must cross the cordon many times.

notes: Facts in the source paraphrase the cited evaluations; an annotator must check dates and numbers against them. The 9:00 vs 15:00 transfer check rests on target facts (arrival peak 8-10, half empty after 14:00). Implied-cue leak checks on place names are marked ambiguous: mentioning Lidingö or Essingeleden in a label is odd but arguably harmless. v2 migration notes: under v2 rules a detail banned only by inference is UNCLEAR unless copying it would be false for the target (only the currency I1 qualifies), so the implied variants and counter-stated-full sit in the ambiguity set until reviewers adjudicate. The counter and wrong-fit T1 checks moved to must_not_transfer because they test a unit the answer must not use. J1 needs the audited semantic judge.
